passages.happening: Jesus tells a story. A man plants a vineyard, builds a wall around it, digs a pit for pressing the grapes, and builds a watchtower. He rents it out to tenant farmers and goes away. At harvest he sends a servant to collect his share of the fruit. The tenants beat the servant and send him away with nothing. He sends another, and they hit him on the head and shame him. He sends another, and they kill him, and many more after that. Last of all he sends his own beloved son. The tenants say, ‘This is the heir. Come, let us kill him, and the inheritance will be ours.’ They kill him and throw his body out of the vineyard. What will the owner do? He will come, destroy those tenants, and give the vineyard to others. Then Jesus quotes a psalm: “The stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone.” The leaders want to arrest him, because they know the story is aimed at them. But they fear the crowd and leave.
passages.hearers:
Jesus' hearers knew this kind of arrangement. An owner would rent out his land to tenant farmers, who paid him a share of the crop.

But Jesus' first words would have rung a much louder bell. His description of the vineyard, the wall, the winepress, and the tower, follows the opening of a famous song in Isaiah 5. In that song the vineyard is Israel, and the owner is God. So the hearers knew at once that the story was about God and his people.

Notice who the story is told against. Jesus is speaking in the temple courts to the chief priests, scribes, and elders who had just questioned his authority (11:27). Mark says the leaders knew the story was about them. The vineyard itself is not the villain. The tenants who were put in charge of it are.
passages.ot:
Isaiah's song begins, “My beloved had a vineyard on a very fertile hill.” The owner “built a watchtower in the middle and dug out a winepress as well” (Isaiah 5:1-2). Then the song explains itself: “For the vineyard of the LORD of Hosts is the house of Israel” (Isaiah 5:7).

The stone saying comes from Psalm 118:22-23, the same psalm the crowd sang as Jesus rode into the city (11:9). A builder rejects a stone as useless, and God makes it the most important stone in the building. The son the tenants threw out will become the cornerstone.
passages.hard: Is this parable saying that God has rejected the Jewish people and given their place to Gentiles? For centuries many Christians read it that way, and that reading was used to justify contempt and worse toward Jews. Many Christian scholars today reject it. Mark says plainly that the story was aimed at the leaders who were in charge of the temple in that hour, and that the Jewish crowd listening was on Jesus' side (verse 12). The ‘others’ who receive the vineyard are, in Mark's story, the new leaders Jesus is gathering, the Twelve, all of them Jews. Readers differ on how far the parable also speaks of the later church, made of Jews and Gentiles together. But the story is a warning to anyone given charge of God's people, not a verdict on a nation.
passages.asks: The tenants wanted the vineyard for themselves. They forgot it was never theirs. Ask what God has put in your care: a family, a gift, a church, a job. Do you treat it as his, and give him the fruit? Or have you started acting as if it belongs to you?

passages.happening: The leaders send some Pharisees and Herodians to catch Jesus in his words. They start with flattery: he is honest, he does not care about anyone's favour, he teaches God's way truly. Then they ask, “Is it lawful to pay taxes to Caesar or not?” Jesus sees through them. He asks them to bring him a denarius, a silver coin. He asks whose image and whose inscription is on it. “Caesar's,” they say. Jesus answers, “Give to Caesar what is Caesar's, and to God what is God's.” They are amazed at him.
passages.hearers:
This was a trap with two jaws. The Pharisees were teachers of the law, popular with ordinary people. The Herodians were supporters of the Herod family, who ruled with Rome's backing. These two groups did not usually work together.

The tax was a sore point. In AD 6 Rome took direct control of Judea and held a census, a count of people and property, so that it could tax them. A man called Judas the Galilean led a revolt against it, teaching that God alone was Israel's master. The book of Acts remembers him (Acts 5:37). So if Jesus said ‘Pay’, many in the crowd would think he had sided with Rome. If he said ‘Don't pay’, he could be reported to the Roman governor as a rebel.

The usual silver denarius of the emperor Tiberius showed his head, crowned with a wreath. Its Latin words called him ‘Tiberius Caesar Augustus, son of the divine Augustus’, and the other side named him ‘high priest’. We cannot be sure which coin they handed Jesus, but a coin like this carried both a human image and a claim to be divine. Notice that Jesus does not have one. His questioners do, right there in the temple courts.
passages.ot: Many readers hear in Jesus' word ‘image’ the first chapter of the Bible, where God made human beings in his own image (Genesis 1:27). They hear the point: the coin bears Caesar's image, so give it to him. You bear God's image, so give yourself to God.
passages.hard:
What does Jesus mean, and how does it apply to Christians and governments? Readers have taken it in more than one way, and Christians in different traditions weigh these differently.

One reading sees two real spheres. Government has a true but limited claim, such as taxes, and God has the greater claim. Paul later writes, “Pay everyone what you owe him: taxes to whom taxes are due” (Romans 13:7). Another reading stresses that the second half swallows the first. Everything belongs to God, Caesar included, so Caesar's claim is small and his claim to be divine is false. A third reading notes that Jesus' answer is clever on purpose. He avoids the trap and leaves his hearers to work out what truly belongs to Caesar.

What all agree on is this. Jesus refused to let either side make him a tool of their cause. And no ruler, of any party, gets what belongs only to God.
passages.asks: The question was meant to force Jesus onto a side. He would not be used. Ask whether you have let a political side take a place in your heart that belongs to God. Then ask the deeper question. You carry God's image. What would it mean to give him all of yourself?

passages.happening: Then some Sadducees come. They say there is no resurrection. They ask about a law of Moses: if a man dies with no children, his brother should marry the widow and raise children for him. Suppose there were seven brothers. Each in turn married the same woman and died with no children. Last of all she died. In the resurrection, whose wife will she be? Jesus says they are mistaken, because they do not know the Scriptures or the power of God. When the dead rise, they do not marry. They are like the angels in heaven. And as for the dead rising, have they not read about the burning bush, where God says, ‘I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob’? He is not the God of the dead, but of the living. “You are badly mistaken!”
passages.hearers:
The Sadducees were a small but powerful group. Acts links the high priest and his circle with them (Acts 5:17). The Jewish historian Josephus says they believed the soul dies with the body, and that they kept only what the written law commanded, not the traditions the Pharisees taught (Antiquities 18.16). Acts adds that they denied the resurrection, angels, and spirits (Acts 23:8).

The law they quote is Deuteronomy 25:5-6. If a man died with no son, his brother was to marry the widow, so that the dead man's name and family line would go on. The book of Ruth shows a related custom.

Their story is meant to make belief in the resurrection look silly. Seven husbands, one wife, one heaven: what a mess. Many Jews of the time did believe God would raise the dead. One Jewish book, 2 Maccabees, tells of seven brothers who died under a cruel king rather than break God's law, trusting that God would raise them to new life (2 Maccabees 7). The Sadducees' seven brothers may be a mocking echo of that story.
passages.ot: Daniel had promised, “many who sleep in the dust of the earth will awake, some to everlasting life” (Daniel 12:2). But Jesus answers from the books of Moses, the part of Scripture the Sadducees held most firmly. At the burning bush, long after Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob had died, God says, “I am the God of your father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob” (Exodus 3:6). God does not say ‘I was’. If he is still their God, they are not finished. A God who keeps his promises will not leave his friends in the grave.
passages.hard:
Does this mean there will be no marriage in heaven, and that husbands and wives will not know each other? Christians read verse 25 in a few ways. Many take it plainly: marriage as we know it belongs to this age, when people die and need children to carry on. In the resurrection no one dies, so the reason for marriage as an institution is gone (compare Luke 20:36). Others stress what Jesus does not say. He does not say love is lost, or that people will not know one another, or that they will become angels. They will be ‘like’ the angels in this one way. Many believers hope that the love of this life will be fulfilled, not erased. The text does not settle every question, and it is wise not to claim more than it says.

For anyone grieving a husband or wife, this verse can feel cold. It is not meant to. Jesus' whole point is that God is the God of the living, and that the dead in him are not lost.
passages.asks: The Sadducees used a puzzle to keep God small. Jesus said their problem was that they did not know the power of God. Ask whether you have made God only as big as what seems possible to you. And if you are grieving, hold on to the name God gave himself: the God of the living.

passages.happening: A scribe, a teacher of the law, has been listening. He sees that Jesus answered well, so he asks, “Which commandment is the most important of all?” Jesus answers with the words every Jew knew: ‘Hear, O Israel, the Lord our God, the Lord is One. Love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind and with all your strength.’ The second is this: ‘Love your neighbor as yourself.’ No commandment is greater than these. The scribe agrees warmly. Loving God and neighbor, he says, matters more than all burnt offerings and sacrifices. Jesus sees that he has answered wisely and tells him, “You are not far from the kingdom of God.” After that no one dares to ask him anything more.
passages.hearers:
The first words are called the Shema, from the Hebrew word for ‘Hear’. It was, and still is, the heart of Jewish prayer. The Mishnah, written down around AD 200, opens with rules for saying it each evening and each morning (Berakhot 1:1). The law itself told Israel to speak these words “when you lie down and when you get up” (Deuteronomy 6:7).

Asking for the heart of the law was a real question among Jewish teachers. The Talmud, written down centuries later, tells of the great teacher Hillel summing up the whole law for a Gentile: what is hateful to you, do not do to your neighbor (Shabbat 31a). A later teacher, Rabbi Akiva, is remembered for calling ‘love your neighbor as yourself’ a great principle of the law.

This scene is warm. Not every scribe is against Jesus. This one listens, agrees, and is praised.
passages.ot:
Jesus joins two verses from different books. Deuteronomy 6:4-5: “Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is One. And you shall love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your strength.” And Leviticus 19:18: “love your neighbor as yourself.”

The scribe's words about sacrifice echo the prophets. Samuel said, “obedience is better than sacrifice” (1 Samuel 15:22), and Hosea, speaking for God, “I desire mercy, not sacrifice” (Hosea 6:6). It is striking that the scribe says this in the temple courts, where sacrifices were offered every day.
passages.asks: Jesus does not give a new commandment here. He gives the oldest ones, and says they hold everything else. Ask whether your faith has become busy with lesser things while love of God and love of neighbour run thin. And notice: being ‘not far’ from the kingdom is not the same as being in it. What would it take for you to take the last step?

passages.happening: Now Jesus asks a question of his own, as he teaches in the temple courts. How can the scribes say that the Christ, the promised king, is the son of David? David himself, speaking by the Holy Spirit, said: ‘The Lord said to my Lord, “Sit at My right hand until I put Your enemies under Your feet.”’ David calls him ‘Lord’. So how can he be David's son? The large crowd listens to him with delight.
passages.hearers:
Everyone agreed that the Messiah would come from David's family. God had promised David a son whose throne would last forever (2 Samuel 7:12-13). Bartimaeus had just called Jesus ‘Son of David’ (10:47), and the crowd at the gate had praised ‘the coming kingdom of our father David’ (11:10).

A father would not normally call his own son ‘lord’. The son honoured the father. So if David calls this future king ‘my Lord’, the king must be more than David's son. Jesus is asking the crowd to think bigger.
passages.ot: Psalm 110:1 reads: “The LORD said to my Lord: ‘Sit at My right hand until I make Your enemies a footstool for Your feet.’” Peter quotes it at Pentecost to show that God has made Jesus “both Lord and Christ” (Acts 2:36).
passages.hard:
Does Jesus' argument depend on David writing the psalm, and is he denying that the Messiah is David's son? Readers answer in different ways. Many modern scholars think Psalm 110 was first written for a king of Judah by a court poet, not by David himself. Others, including many evangelical and Catholic scholars, hold to David as its author, as the psalm's heading says. A third view holds that Jesus argued from what his hearers already accepted, whoever first wrote the psalm, and that his point stands either way.

On the second question, Jesus does not deny that the Messiah is David's son. Mark has just let Bartimaeus call him that with no correction. Jesus asks how the Messiah can be both David's son and David's Lord. The early Christians answered with the resurrection. Paul says Jesus was “a descendant of David according to the flesh” and was “declared with power to be the Son of God by His resurrection from the dead” (Romans 1:3-4).
passages.asks: It is easy to fit Jesus into a title we already understand. Jesus pushes back: he is more than you think. Ask whether your picture of Jesus has grown smaller than he is, and what it would mean to call him ‘Lord’ and not only ‘teacher’ or ‘example’.

passages.happening: In his teaching Jesus warns the crowd about the scribes. They like to walk around in long robes and be greeted with respect in the marketplaces. They like the best seats in the synagogues and the places of honour at banquets. They eat up widows' houses, and for a show they make long prayers. They will receive the heavier judgment.
passages.hearers:
Scribes were trained experts in the law of Moses, and people looked up to them. Their long robes set them apart in a crowd.

How did they ‘defraud widows of their houses’? Mark does not say. Scholars have suggested ways, such as charging for legal help, or mismanaging property they held in trust for a widow. We do not know which, and it may have been more than one.

Jesus is not condemning every scribe. A few verses earlier he told a scribe that he was not far from the kingdom of God (verse 34). His warning is about a kind of religious leader, found in every faith and every age, who loves honour and uses his position to take from the weak.
passages.ot: Widows were God's special concern in the law. “You must not mistreat any widow or orphan” (Exodus 22:22). Isaiah condemned leaders who “make widows their prey and orphans their plunder” (Isaiah 10:2).
passages.asks: This warning is first for those who lead and teach in the church today, who also have robes, titles, and seats of honour. Ask whether you love being seen as godly more than being godly. And ask who the ‘widows’ are around you: the people with no one to defend them. Are you protecting them or ignoring them?

passages.happening: Jesus sits down opposite the place where offerings are given and watches the crowd putting money in. Many rich people put in large amounts. Then a poor widow comes and puts in two small copper coins, worth only a tiny part of a denarius. Jesus calls his disciples over. Truly, he says, this poor widow has put in more than all the others. They gave out of what they had left over. She, out of her poverty, has put in everything she had to live on.
passages.hearers:
The Mishnah describes thirteen offering chests in the temple, shaped like trumpets, narrow at the top and wide at the bottom, each marked for a different purpose (Shekalim 6:5). The Mishnah was written down more than a century after the temple fell, so its details may not all fit Jesus' day, but it gives a picture of the kind of place where the widow gave.

Her two coins were the smallest coins in use in that land. Mark explains them for Roman readers: two of them made a quadrans, the smallest Roman coin. It took sixty-four of those to make one denarius, a day's wage. Her gift was worth a few minutes of a labourer's work.

A widow was often among the poorest people in the land, with no husband to provide for her and no one to defend her rights. And Jesus has just warned about men who ‘defraud widows of their houses’ (verse 40).
passages.hard:
Does Jesus praise the widow, or grieve over what was done to her? Most readers through the centuries have heard praise. Jesus calls his disciples to him and says solemnly that she gave more than all the rest, because she gave everything. Her gift points ahead to Jesus himself, who will soon give his whole life.

In 1982 the scholar Addison Wright argued for another reading. The story comes right after Jesus condemns those who devour widows' houses, and right before he says the temple will be torn down (13:2). Jesus never says she did well or tells anyone to copy her. So, Wright argued, Jesus is lamenting that a system had taught a poor woman to give her last coins to a temple about to fall. Others have answered that this reading is clever but misses the plain tone. Many readers now hold both: Jesus honours her real and costly devotion, and he condemns leaders who should have been caring for her instead of taking from her.

What the story does not teach is that the poor must give away what they need to live, or that God's favour can be bought.
passages.asks: God measures a gift by what it costs, not by its size. Ask what you give God from your leftovers, and whether there is anything you give that truly costs you. And if you are a leader, ask whether anyone in your care is giving out of need while you look away.
